lessons.title: Cinnamon and Nutmeg in Baked Goods
lessons.body: Cinnamon and nutmeg are the workhorses of African baking. In West Africa, cinnamon bark is often sold in long quills; in East Africa, ground cinnamon is more common. For a standard loaf cake or 12 muffins, start with 1 teaspoon of ground cinnamon and 1/4 teaspoon of ground nutmeg. If you grate whole nutmeg, use a fine graterâone whole nutmeg yields about 2 teaspoons. Always buy whole nutmeg and grate fresh; pre-ground nutmeg loses its oils in weeks. Cinnamon sticks can be steeped in milk for custards: warm 500 ml milk with 2 sticks for 10 minutes, then remove. For a classic banana bread, mash 3 ripe bananas, mix with 100 g sugar, 1 egg, 60 ml oil, 200 g flour, 1 tsp baking soda, 1 tsp cinnamon, 1/4 tsp nutmeg, and 1/2 tsp salt. Bake at 180Â°C for 50â60 minutes. In South Africa, cinnamon is used in melktert (milk tart) and koeksisters. For melktert, infuse 500 ml milk with 1 cinnamon stick, then thicken with 3 tbsp cornflour and 2 egg yolks. Top with cinnamon sugar. Nutmeg pairs well with pumpkin and sweet potato in pies. For a pumpkin pie, add 1/2 tsp nutmeg and 1 tsp cinnamon to 2 cups mashed pumpkin, 2 eggs, 200 ml condensed milk, and 100 g sugar. Bake in a blind-baked crust at 180Â°C for 45 minutes. Remember: cinnamon burns easily, so reduce oven temperature by 10Â°C if your recipe calls for a long bake. Store ground spices in airtight jars away from sunlight. In Africa, many home bakers use cinnamon in tea and coffee, but for baking, always measureâtoo much cinnamon makes dough bitter. Start with these ratios and adjust to your taste. Practice with a simple cinnamon roll recipe: dough of 500 g flour, 7 g yeast, 250 ml warm milk, 50 g sugar, 1 egg, 50 g butter. Filling: 100 g soft butter, 100 g brown sugar, 2 tbsp cinnamon. Roll, cut, bake at 190Â°C for 20 minutes. This module will give you the confidence to use these spices daily.

lessons.title: Cardamom in Sweet Dishes
lessons.body: Cardamom is the queen of sweet spices in Africa, especially in North and East African desserts. Green cardamom pods are preferred for sweets; black cardamom is smoky and used in savoury dishes. To use green cardamom, crack the pods with the back of a knife and remove the small black seeds. Grind the seeds fresh in a mortar or spice grinder. One teaspoon of ground cardamom requires about 12â15 pods. For a simple cardamom cake, cream 200 g butter with 200 g sugar, add 4 eggs one at a time, then fold in 250 g flour, 1 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp ground cardamom, and 100 ml milk. Bake at 170Â°C for 40 minutes. In Egypt, cardamom is used in basbousa (semolina cake): mix 300 g semolina, 100 g sugar, 1 tsp cardamom, 200 ml yoghurt, 100 g melted butter, and 1 tsp baking powder. Spread in a tray, bake at 180Â°C for 30 minutes, then pour over sugar syrup (200 g sugar + 150 ml water boiled with 2 cardamom pods). In Ethiopia, cardamom is added to coffee and sometimes to sweet breads. For a quick dessert, make cardamom rice pudding: simmer 100 g rice in 500 ml milk with 4 crushed cardamom pods, 50 g sugar, and a pinch of salt for 25 minutes. Stir in 1 tbsp butter. Serve warm. Cardamom also works in fruit salads: sprinkle ground cardamom over sliced oranges, dates, and bananas with a squeeze of lime. For chocolate-cardamom truffles, melt 200 g dark chocolate, mix with 100 ml cream, 1/2 tsp ground cardamom, and 1 tbsp butter. Chill, roll into balls, and coat in cocoa. Cardamom is strongâuse sparingly. A little goes a long way. Always taste your batter before baking. If you cannot find green pods, use ground cardamom but reduce amount by half because it is more concentrated. Store pods in an airtight jar; they keep their flavour for up to a year. In African markets, cardamom is often sold in bulkâbuy small quantities and grind as needed. With practice, you will learn to balance cardamom with other spices like cinnamon and nutmeg.

lessons.title: Ginger in Cookies and Cakes
lessons.body: Ginger brings warmth and zing to African baked goods. Fresh ginger root is widely available; dried ground ginger is convenient. For cookies, ground ginger is best because fresh ginger adds too much moisture. A classic ginger cookie recipe: cream 100 g butter with 150 g brown sugar, add 1 egg, 2 tbsp molasses (or honey), then mix in 250 g flour, 1 tsp baking soda, 1 tbsp ground ginger, 1 tsp cinnamon, 1/2 tsp cloves, and 1/4 tsp salt. Roll dough into balls, flatten, bake at 180Â°C for 12 minutes. For a softer cake, try ginger cake: 200 g flour, 150 g sugar, 1 tsp baking powder, 2 tsp ground ginger, 1/2 tsp nutmeg, 2 eggs, 120 ml oil, 120 ml milk, and 2 tbsp grated fresh ginger. Bake at 170Â°C for 45 minutes. In Nigeria and Ghana, ginger is used in chin chin and puff-puff sometimes. For a spiced ginger loaf, add 100 g chopped dates or raisins. Fresh ginger can be juiced: grate 100 g ginger, squeeze through a cloth to get 2 tbsp juice, and add to cake batter for a punch. In South Africa, ginger is used in ginger beer (a fermented drink) and in koeksisters syrup. For a simple dessert, poach pear slices in a syrup of 200 g sugar, 500 ml water, 2 tbsp grated ginger, and 1 cinnamon stick for 15 minutes. Serve with ice cream. Ginger also pairs well with chocolate: add 1 tsp ground ginger to your favourite brownie recipe. Always measure ground ginger carefullyâtoo much can be bitter. If using fresh ginger in baking, grate it finely and increase liquid slightly. Store fresh ginger in the fridge for up to 3 weeks or freeze for 6 months. Ground ginger should be replaced every 6 months for best flavour. Practice with a small batch first. For a quick microwave mug cake: mix 4 tbsp flour, 2 tbsp sugar, 1/4 tsp baking powder, 1/4 tsp ground ginger, 3 tbsp milk, 1 tbsp oil, and microwave for 1 minute. This is a great way to test ginger intensity. Remember, ginger is a stimulant; in moderation, it aids digestion. Use it in cookies for tea time or in cakes for celebrations.

lessons.title: Cloves and Allspice in Pies and Preserves
lessons.body: Cloves and allspice are bold spices that shine in pies and preserves. Cloves are dried flower buds; allspice is a dried berry that tastes like a mix of cinnamon, nutmeg, and cloves. In Africa, cloves are grown in Tanzania and Madagascar. For apple pie, use 1/4 teaspoon ground cloves and 1/2 teaspoon ground allspice per 1 kg of sliced apples, along with 100 g sugar, 2 tbsp flour, and 1 tbsp lemon juice. Bake in a double crust at 200Â°C for 45 minutes. For pumpkin pie, add 1/4 tsp cloves and 1/2 tsp allspice to the filling. In preserves, cloves are used in pickled fruits and chutneys. For a simple pear preserve: peel and core 1 kg pears, cut into chunks, and simmer with 500 g sugar, 200 ml water, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 6 whole cloves, and 1 cinnamon stick for 30 minutes until thick. Pour into sterilised jars. Allspice is key in Jamaican jerk seasoning, but for sweets, it works in spice cakes. For a spiced plum pie: mix 800 g pitted plums with 100 g sugar, 2 tbsp cornflour, 1/2 tsp allspice, 1/4 tsp cloves, and 1/2 tsp cinnamon. Bake in a crust at 190Â°C for 40 minutes. Cloves are very strongânever use more than 1/4 tsp ground in a standard pie. Whole cloves can be removed before serving. In Morocco, cloves are used in sweet pastries like briouat. For a quick dessert, make spiced baked apples: core 4 apples, fill with 2 tbsp brown sugar, 1/4 tsp allspice, and 2 whole cloves. Bake at 180Â°C for 25 minutes. Allspice berries can be ground fresh; 1 tsp whole berries yields about 1/2 tsp ground. Store whole cloves and allspice berries in airtight jars; they last for years. Ground versions lose flavour in 6 months. When making preserves, always sterilise jars by boiling for 10 minutes. Use a candy thermometer to check setting point (105Â°C). These spices also work in meat pies, but for desserts, balance with sugar. Practice with a small apple pie first. In African markets, cloves are sold in small packets; buy whole and grind as needed. Allspice is sometimes called 'pimento' in the Caribbean. With these spices, your pies will have a deep, warm flavour.

lessons.title: Vanilla and Spice Combinations
lessons.body: Vanilla is the most popular flavour in baking, but it becomes magical when combined with spices. In Africa, vanilla is grown in Madagascar, Uganda, and Comoros. Vanilla extract is made by steeping split vanilla beans in alcohol (vodka or rum) for 8 weeks. For a quick version, use 1 vanilla bean per 100 ml alcohol. In baking, 1 teaspoon of vanilla extract is standard for a cake or 12 cookies. Vanilla pairs well with cinnamon, nutmeg, cardamom, and ginger. For a spiced vanilla cake: cream 200 g butter with 200 g sugar, add 3 eggs, 2 tsp vanilla extract, then fold in 250 g flour, 1 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp cinnamon, 1/2 tsp nutmeg, and 1/4 tsp cardamom. Bake at 170Â°C for 45 minutes. For a vanilla-spice pound cake, add 1/2 tsp ground ginger and 1/4 tsp cloves. In custards, vanilla and nutmeg are classic: warm 500 ml milk with 1 split vanilla bean and a grating of nutmeg, then whisk into 4 egg yolks and 100 g sugar, cook until thickened. For a quick dessert, make vanilla-spice poached peaches: simmer 4 halved peaches in 500 ml water, 200 g sugar, 1 vanilla bean, 1 cinnamon stick, and 2 cardamom pods for 10 minutes. Serve with cream. Vanilla also enhances chocolate: add 1 tsp vanilla and 1/2 tsp cinnamon to brownies. In Africa, vanilla is expensive, so use it wisely. Vanilla powder (ground beans) is potentâuse half the amount of extract. Vanilla paste has seeds and extract; use 1 tsp. Always add vanilla extract after removing from heat if using in hot liquids, as heat can diminish flavour. For a spice blend, mix 2 tbsp cinnamon, 1 tbsp nutmeg, 1 tbsp ginger, 1 tsp cloves, and 1 tsp cardamom; add 1 tsp of this blend to your vanilla cakes. Store vanilla beans in an airtight jar away from light; they last for 2 years. Make your own extract to save money: split 6 beans, place in a 500 ml bottle, fill with rum, and shake weekly for 2 months. This module will help you create signature flavours. Remember, vanilla is a flavour enhancerâit makes other spices taste better. Start with small amounts and adjust.

lessons.title: Spiced Beverages: Chai, Mulled Wine, and More
lessons.body: Spiced beverages are a delicious way to enjoy spices. Chai is popular in East Africa, especially Kenya and Tanzania. For a basic chai: boil 500 ml water with 2 crushed cardamom pods, 1 cinnamon stick, 3 cloves, 1 slice fresh ginger, and 1 star anise for 5 minutes. Add 2 black tea bags and 250 ml milk, then simmer for 3 minutes. Sweeten with sugar or honey. For mulled wine (or mulled grape juice for non-alcoholic), heat 750 ml red wine (or grape juice) with 2 cinnamon sticks, 4 cloves, 2 star anise, 1 orange sliced, 2 tbsp honey, and 1/4 tsp nutmeg. Simmer gently for 15 minutesâdo not boil. Serve warm. In North Africa, spiced coffee is common: add 1/4 tsp cinnamon, 1/4 tsp cardamom, and a pinch of nutmeg to ground coffee before brewing. For a spiced hot chocolate: heat 500 ml milk with 1 cinnamon stick, 2 cloves, and 1/4 tsp cardamom for 5 minutes, then whisk in 100 g chopped dark chocolate and 1 tbsp sugar. For a cold option, make spiced iced tea: brew 4 black tea bags in 1 litre water with 1 cinnamon stick, 3 cardamom pods, and 1 slice ginger. Chill, then serve over ice with lemon. In West Africa, ginger drink (known as 'ginger beer' but non-alcoholic) is made by blending 200 g fresh ginger with 1 litre water, straining, and adding sugar and cloves to taste. For a quick spiced lemonade: mix juice of 4 lemons with 1 litre water, 100 g sugar, 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon, and 1/4 tsp ground cloves. Always strain whole spices before serving. Use a fine mesh sieve or cheesecloth. For mulled wine, avoid boiling to keep alcohol. For chai, you can use tea leaves instead of bags. Adjust spices to your tasteâstart with less and add more. These beverages are perfect for gatherings. In Africa, chai is often sold by street vendors; you can make it at home for a fraction of the cost. Store leftover mulled wine in the fridge for up to 3 days; reheat gently. For a party, set up a chai station with cinnamon sticks, cardamom pods, and ginger for guests to customise. Practice with a small batch first. Remember, whole spices are best for beverages; ground spices can make drinks cloudy. With these recipes, you can warm up any occasion.
